column1: What is the 'picture plane' in perspective drawing, and what is its key invariant relative to the observer?
column2: An imaginary transparent vertical surface (like a pane of glass) between the observer and the scene onto which all objects project. It remains stationary relative to the observer, and projection lines pass through it at right angles to the observer's line of sight.

column1: What does the horizon line actually represent, and why is it NOT the same as where sky meets earth?
column2: The horizon line represents the observer's eye level extended infinitely across the picture plane. It persists in interiors, still lifes, and figure studies—it only happens to coincide with the visible sky-earth boundary in open landscapes.

column1: What is the single geometric invariant underlying all vanishing point systems?
column2: Parallel lines in 3D space that recede into depth converge to a common vanishing point when projected onto the picture plane—a necessity of fixed viewpoint and straight-line light travel, not an artistic convention.

column1: What determines whether a drawing requires one, two, or three vanishing points?
column2: The orientation of the subject relative to the picture plane: one face parallel to the canvas = 1 VP; two faces at oblique angles = 2 VPs; tilting the form up/down adds a 3rd VP for vertical convergence.

column1: In one- and two-point perspective, why do vertical lines remain perfectly vertical instead of converging?
column2: Because they are perpendicular to the picture plane, which is itself untilted, so verticals stay parallel to each other with no convergence.

column1: What causes vertical lines to converge to a third vanishing point?
column2: Three-point perspective occurs when the picture plane itself is tilted (e.g., viewer looking sharply up or down), causing verticals to converge above or below the horizon.

column1: What is the proportional compression rule for a cube's far edge versus its near edge on the ground plane?
column2: If the far edge is twice as distant from the viewer as the near edge, the far edge's apparent height will be exactly half that of the near edge—governed by the inverse relationship between apparent size and distance in central projection.

column1: Why must every vanishing point governing horizontal recession lie on the horizon line?
column2: Because horizontal parallel lines in the world remain horizontal relative to the observer's eye level, so their convergence points must sit on that eye-level line (the horizon).

column1: In two-point perspective, what happens to a square tile on the ground plane when projected?
column2: It becomes a quadrilateral with four different edge lengths (not a square), yet the overall grid system remains mathematically coherent as it recedes toward two vanishing points simultaneously.

column1: What effect does placing vanishing points close together have on a drawing?
column2: It produces extreme foreshortening and optical distortion (a 'fish-eye' effect), simulating a very wide-angle or close-up viewpoint.

column1: What is the core invariant principle behind advanced compositional use of perspective?
column2: Every element in a composition exists within a spatial envelope defined by the viewer's position and the recession of the picture plane—objects occupy measurable positions relative to the horizon line, vanishing points, and eye level rather than floating in abstract space.

column1: During the 'Box Sprint' drill, why should vanishing points be placed outside the canvas boundaries when working digitally?
column2: To avoid extreme distortion (the fish-eye effect) that occurs when vanishing points are too close together relative to the drawn form.
